# PART 3 – Individual effects and aggregate associations {#part-3-individual-effects-and-aggregate-associations .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 3
:::

::: notes
Part three asks the question that the panel could not answer. When unemployment rises in a country and framing falls, is that because the context changed for everyone, or because the mix of people in the sample changed? The multilevel model holds both coefficients at once, the effect of being unemployed oneself and the association with the national rate, and a short piece of arithmetic says how much of the second the first could explain.
:::

## Context and composition {#context-and-composition .smaller}

::: {.small}
- In the published model without its interactions, with countries and country-waves as its levels, fitted to the real respondents, being unemployed rather than a manual worker moves the cosmopolitan score by `r fmt_num(b_ind, 4)`, and one point of the national rate by `r fmt_num(b_ctx, 5)`, net of who the respondent is
- The two coefficients apply to different units. The individual effect applies to whoever is unemployed; the coefficient on the national rate, with the status of the respondent held constant, applies to everyone, and it is what multilevel modellers call a contextual effect
- Contextual effects, "of enduring interest in organizational sociology", occur "when the aggregate of a person-level characteristic ... is related to the outcome ... even after controlling for the effect of the individual characteristic" [@RaudenbushBryk2002HierarchicalLinearModels, p. 139]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Composition could explain the national association only if the national rate changes who is in the sample: the **prevalence gradient**.
:::

::: notes
Here are the two coefficients side by side, from the published model without its interactions, fitted once to the real respondents. Being unemployed yourself moves your cosmopolitan score by about three and a half points of share, and one point of the national rate moves everyone's score by about half a point, net of who they are. Per unit, the individual effect is between six and seven times the size. But the two numbers apply to different people. The first applies to whoever is unemployed. The second, with the status of each respondent held constant, applies to everyone, and Raudenbush and Bryk call such a coefficient a contextual effect. [advance] The people who lost their jobs could explain the national association only if a higher national rate puts noticeably more unemployed people into the sample, and that quantity, the prevalence gradient, can be measured.
:::

## The arithmetic of composition {#the-arithmetic-of-composition .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: d3-composition-table
# The compositional path with the coefficients of the real respondents
# (companion/_model-outputs/anchor_person_fixed.csv) and the
# prevalence gradient within country and year
# (companion/_model-outputs/prevalence_gradient.csv)
tibble::tibble(
  Quantity = c("The effect of being unemployed", "The extra unemployed share for each point of the national rate",
               "The compositional contribution to the national slope", "The national slope itself",
               "The compositional share of the national slope"),
  Value = c(fmt_num(b_ind, 4), fmt_num(grad_w, 4), fmt_num(b_ind * grad_w, 5), fmt_num(b_ctx, 5),
            fmt_pct(b_ind * grad_w / b_ctx))
) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

::: {.small}
- A rise of one point in the national rate adds well under one percentage point to the share of respondents who are themselves unemployed, so an effect several times the size, spread over a group that barely grows, moves the national average hardly at all
- The calculation needs an individual effect *and* a prevalence gradient, and the second is usually assumed, although it can be measured. Ask for it whenever an aggregate association is explained by 'it must be the people who changed'
:::

::: {.src}
companion/multilevel.qmd, section 6; companion/_model-outputs/anchor_person_fixed.csv and prevalence_gradient.csv.
:::

::: notes
The arithmetic is short. A point more of national unemployment adds well under one percentage point to the share of respondents who are themselves unemployed. Multiply that by the individual effect, and the compositional path contributes a tiny amount to the national slope: less than five per cent of it. An effect several times the size, spread over a group that barely grows, moves the average hardly at all. So the national association is not a matter of who was interviewed, and the contextual reading survives. The calculation is worth asking for whenever someone explains an aggregate association by saying that it must be the people who changed. It needs two numbers, the individual effect and the prevalence gradient, and the second is usually assumed rather than measured.
:::
